CHAPTER 9 - MOTION AND ITS DESCRIPTION

Introduction

We see motion everywhere: a bus moving on a road, a bird flying, blood flowing in our veins, the Earth revolving around the Sun. The branch of physics that describes motion without worrying about its causes is called KINEMATICS. In this chapter we build the vocabulary and the mathematics needed to describe motion precisely - rest and motion, distance and displacement, speed and velocity, acceleration, the three equations of motion, and the graphs that picture motion.

9.1 REST AND MOTION ARE RELATIVE - FRAME OF REFERENCE

An object is said to be at REST if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings, and in MOTION if its position changes with time. But position must always be measured with respect to some chosen point or object called the ORIGIN or the FRAME OF REFERENCE. Rest and motion are therefore RELATIVE terms - they depend on the observer's frame.
Consider a passenger sitting in a moving train. Relative to the seat and to a fellow passenger, she is at rest. Relative to a person standing on the platform, she is moving at the speed of the train. Neither description is wrong; each is correct in its own frame of reference. There is no such thing as 'absolute rest' - even the platform is carried along by the rotating, orbiting Earth. To describe motion we first fix a frame of reference (often the ground) and a coordinate system attached to it.

9.2 POINT OBJECT (POINT MASS)

When the size of a body is very small compared with the distance it travels, we can treat the body as a single point - a POINT OBJECT. For example, a train travelling between two cities hundreds of kilometres apart can be treated as a point, because its length (a few hundred metres) is negligible compared with the journey. Treating a body as a point object simplifies the description of its motion, since we then need to track only one position, not the motion of every part.

9.3 SCALAR AND VECTOR QUANTITIES

Physical quantities are of two kinds.
 - A SCALAR quantity has only MAGNITUDE (a number with a unit). Examples: distance, speed, mass, time, temperature, energy.
 - A VECTOR quantity has BOTH magnitude AND direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum.
Two vectors are equal only if they have the same magnitude AND the same direction. This distinction is central to describing motion correctly: speed is a scalar but velocity is a vector; distance is a scalar but displacement is a vector.

9.4 DISTANCE AND DISPLACEMENT

DISTANCE is the total length of the actual path travelled by a body, regardless of direction. It is a SCALAR, is always positive, and can never decrease. Its SI unit is the metre (m).
DISPLACEMENT is the shortest (straight-line) distance from the initial position to the final position, measured in a definite direction. It is a VECTOR. Its magnitude can be less than the distance, and it can be zero or even 'negative' (i.e. directed opposite to the chosen positive direction). Its SI unit is also the metre (m).
Example: A boy walks 4 m east and then 3 m north. The distance travelled is 4 + 3 = 7 m. The displacement is the straight line from start to finish, of magnitude sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25) = 5 m, directed north-east.
Special case: if a body moves along a closed path and returns to its starting point (for example one full lap of a circular track), the distance equals the circumference but the displacement is ZERO, because the start and end positions coincide. Displacement equals distance only when the motion is along a straight line without reversing direction.

9.5 SPEED

SPEED is the distance travelled per unit time. It is a SCALAR.
   speed = distance / time
The SI unit of speed is metre per second (m/s); another common unit is km/h, with 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s and 1 m/s = 18/5 km/h.
 - UNIFORM SPEED: a body has uniform speed if it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small the intervals.
 - NON-UNIFORM (variable) SPEED: the body covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time.
AVERAGE SPEED is the total distance divided by the total time taken:
   average speed = total distance / total time
Average speed smooths out the variations and gives a single representative value for a whole journey.

9.6 VELOCITY

VELOCITY is the displacement per unit time - the rate of change of displacement. It is a VECTOR, having both magnitude and direction.
   velocity = displacement / time
The SI unit is m/s. The magnitude of velocity in a straight line without reversal equals the speed, but in general the (average) speed and the magnitude of (average) velocity differ, because distance differs from displacement.
AVERAGE VELOCITY = total displacement / total time. For motion with uniformly changing velocity, the average velocity also equals (initial velocity + final velocity)/2 = (u + v)/2.
A body has UNIFORM VELOCITY if it moves in a straight line with constant speed (so neither magnitude nor direction changes). If either the speed or the direction changes, the velocity is non-uniform.

9.7 ACCELERATION

ACCELERATION is the rate of change of velocity with time. It is a VECTOR.
   acceleration = change in velocity / time taken = (v - u) / t
where u is the initial velocity and v is the final velocity. The SI unit of acceleration is metre per second squared (m/s^2).
 - UNIFORM ACCELERATION: the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time (acceleration constant in magnitude and direction). A freely falling body has uniform acceleration g (about 9.8 m/s^2).
 - NON-UNIFORM ACCELERATION: the velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals.
 - POSITIVE acceleration: velocity increases with time (the body speeds up).
 - NEGATIVE acceleration, also called RETARDATION or DECELERATION: velocity decreases with time (the body slows down); acceleration is directed opposite to the motion.
If a body moves with constant velocity, its acceleration is zero.

9.8 THE THREE EQUATIONS OF MOTION (for uniform acceleration)

For a body moving in a straight line with uniform acceleration a, starting with initial velocity u, reaching final velocity v after time t, and covering displacement s, three equations connect these quantities:
   (1)  v = u + a t                 (velocity-time relation)
   (2)  s = u t + (1/2) a t^2        (position-time relation)
   (3)  v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s            (velocity-position relation)
Meaning of the symbols: u = initial velocity (m/s); v = final velocity (m/s); a = uniform acceleration (m/s^2); t = time interval (s); s = displacement during that time (m).
These equations apply ONLY when the acceleration is uniform. For retardation, a is given a negative sign. For a body starting from rest, u = 0, which simplifies the equations.

Worked example 1: A car starting from rest accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s^2 for 5 s. Find its final velocity and the distance covered.
  u = 0, a = 2 m/s^2, t = 5 s.
  v = u + a t = 0 + 2 x 5 = 10 m/s.
  s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 = 0 + (1/2)(2)(5^2) = 25 m.

Worked example 2: A bus moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 4 s by applying brakes. Find the retardation and the distance travelled before stopping.
  u = 20 m/s, v = 0, t = 4 s.
  a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 20)/4 = -5 m/s^2 (retardation of 5 m/s^2).
  s = (u + v)/2 x t = (20 + 0)/2 x 4 = 40 m. (Check with v^2 = u^2 + 2as: 0 = 400 + 2(-5)s => s = 40 m.)

9.9 GRAPHICAL REPRESENTATION OF MOTION

Graphs give a powerful visual description of motion. Time is usually plotted on the x-axis.

(a) DISTANCE-TIME (or position-time) GRAPH.
 - For a body AT REST, the distance-time graph is a straight horizontal line (distance does not change).
 - For UNIFORM SPEED, the graph is a straight line sloping upward; equal distances are covered in equal times. The SLOPE of a distance-time graph gives the SPEED of the body: speed = (change in distance)/(change in time). A steeper line means a greater speed.
 - For NON-UNIFORM speed, the graph is a curve; the speed at any instant equals the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.

(b) VELOCITY-TIME GRAPH.
 - For UNIFORM VELOCITY (zero acceleration), the graph is a straight horizontal line.
 - For UNIFORM ACCELERATION, the graph is a straight sloping line. The SLOPE of a velocity-time graph gives the ACCELERATION: acceleration = (change in velocity)/(change in time).
 - The AREA under a velocity-time graph (between the line and the time axis) gives the DISTANCE (displacement) covered in that interval. For a body accelerating uniformly from u to v in time t, the area is a trapezium of area (1/2)(u + v) t, which equals the displacement s - this is how the equations of motion can be derived graphically.

9.10 UNIFORM CIRCULAR MOTION - AN ACCELERATED MOTION

When a body moves along a circular path with constant SPEED, its motion is called UNIFORM CIRCULAR MOTION. Although the speed is constant, the DIRECTION of motion changes continuously (it is always along the tangent to the circle). Because velocity is a vector that includes direction, a continuous change of direction means the velocity is continuously changing - so the body is ACCELERATING, even though its speed never changes. This is an important example showing that an object can be accelerated without changing its speed. The speed of a body moving in a circle of radius r and completing one revolution in time T (the period) is v = 2 pi r / T, the circumference divided by the time for one round.

SUMMARY

- Rest and motion are relative; they must be described with respect to a chosen frame of reference. There is no absolute rest.
- A small body relative to its path can be treated as a point object.
- Scalars have magnitude only (distance, speed); vectors have magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration).
- Distance is the actual path length (scalar, always >= 0); displacement is the straight-line change in position (vector); for a closed loop displacement is zero.
- Speed = distance/time (scalar); velocity = displacement/time (vector); average speed = total distance/total time; average velocity = total displacement/total time = (u+v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
- Acceleration = (v - u)/t (m/s^2); negative acceleration is retardation.
- Equations of motion (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
- Distance-time graph slope = speed; velocity-time graph slope = acceleration, and the area under it = distance covered.
- Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing direction, so it is accelerated motion.

chapter_summary.title: Motion and its Description - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 9 covers how we describe motion: rest and motion as relative ideas, distance versus displacement, speed and velocity, acceleration, the three equations of motion, and the graphs that picture motion.

branches.label: Frame of reference
details: Point object: size negligible vs path

sections.heading: Rest, motion and frame of reference
bullets: A body is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings, and in motion if its position changes.
Rest and motion are relative: a passenger is at rest relative to the train but moving relative to the platform. There is no absolute rest.
Position is always measured from a chosen origin / frame of reference. A small body compared with its path is treated as a point object.

sections.heading: Scalars, vectors, distance and displacement
bullets: A scalar has only magnitude (distance, speed, mass, time); a vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force).
Distance is the total length of the actual path (scalar, always positive); displacement is the straight-line change of position in a definite direction (vector).
For a closed path, distance equals the perimeter but displacement is zero; displacement equals distance only for straight-line motion without reversing.

sections.heading: Speed and velocity
bullets: Speed = distance/time (scalar); SI unit m/s; 1 m/s = 18/5 km/h. Uniform speed covers equal distances in equal times; otherwise non-uniform.
Average speed = total distance / total time.
Velocity = displacement/time (vector). Average velocity = total displacement/total time = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration. Uniform velocity = constant speed in a straight line.

sections.heading: Acceleration and equations of motion
bullets: Acceleration = rate of change of velocity = (v - u)/t (vector); SI unit m/s^2. Negative acceleration is called retardation (the body slows down).
For uniform acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as, where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = displacement.
These equations hold only when the acceleration is constant; for a body starting from rest, u = 0.

sections.heading: Graphs of motion and circular motion
bullets: The slope of a distance-time graph gives the speed; a horizontal line means the body is at rest, a steeper line means greater speed.
The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the acceleration, and the area under the graph gives the distance (displacement) covered.
In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes and the motion is accelerated.

key_takeaways: Rest and motion are relative and must be described relative to a chosen frame of reference.
Distance is a scalar (path length); displacement is a vector (shortest path); displacement is zero over a closed loop.
Speed = distance/time (scalar); velocity = displacement/time (vector); average speed = total distance/total time.
Acceleration = (v - u)/t in m/s^2; negative acceleration is retardation.
The three equations of motion (v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as) apply only for uniform acceleration.
Distance-time slope = speed; velocity-time slope = acceleration; area under a velocity-time graph = distance.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing direction, hence it is accelerated motion.

glossary.definition: The state of a body whose position does not change with time relative to its surroundings (frame of reference).
The state of a body whose position changes with time relative to a chosen frame of reference.
A chosen object or origin (with a coordinate system) relative to which the position and motion of a body are described.
A body whose size is negligible compared with the distance it travels, so it can be treated as a single point.
A physical quantity having only magnitude, such as distance, speed, mass or time.
A physical quantity having both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration or force.
The total length of the actual path travelled by a body; a scalar quantity that is always positive. SI unit: metre.
The shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position, in a definite direction; a vector. SI unit: metre.
The distance travelled per unit time; a scalar quantity. SI unit: metre per second (m/s).
The displacement per unit time (rate of change of displacement); a vector quantity. SI unit: m/s.
The total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey.
The rate of change of velocity with time, equal to (v - u)/t; a vector. SI unit: metre per second squared (m/s^2).
Negative acceleration; the velocity decreases with time and acceleration is directed opposite to the motion.
For uniform acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at^2 and v^2 = u^2 + 2as, relating u, v, a, t and s.
Motion along a circular path at constant speed; the direction changes continuously, so the motion is accelerated.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Motion and its Description (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) Worksheet-9 for Lesson 9. Attempt all questions. Take g = 9.8 m/s^2 where needed and show all steps for numerical problems.

questions.question: Explain, with an example, why rest and motion are said to be relative terms.
questions.answer:
Rest and motion always depend on the frame of reference (the observer's surroundings) chosen to describe them.
Example: A passenger sitting in a moving train is at REST relative to the seat and to fellow passengers (her position does not change with respect to them). At the same time she is in MOTION relative to a person standing on the platform, because her position changes with respect to him. Both statements are correct in their own frames. Since the same body can be at rest in one frame and moving in another, rest and motion are relative. There is no 'absolute rest', because even the platform and the ground are carried along by the rotating and orbiting Earth.
questions.explanation: Define rest/motion relative to a frame and give the train-platform example.

questions.question: Distinguish between distance and displacement, giving one example where they differ.
questions.answer:
Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by a body. It is a SCALAR (magnitude only), is always positive, and never decreases. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position in a definite direction. It is a VECTOR (magnitude and direction); its magnitude can be less than the distance and can be zero.
Example: A boy walks 4 m east and then 3 m north. Distance = 4 + 3 = 7 m. Displacement = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25) = 5 m, directed north-east. Another example: one full lap of a circular track gives a distance equal to the circumference but a displacement of zero, because the start and finish points coincide.
questions.explanation: Scalar vs vector; path length vs shortest path; example with 4 m and 3 m.

questions.question: Define acceleration. What is meant by negative acceleration (retardation)? Give its SI unit.
questions.answer:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. If the velocity changes from u to v in time t, then acceleration a = (v - u)/t. It is a vector quantity and its SI unit is metre per second squared (m/s^2).
Negative acceleration, also called RETARDATION or deceleration, occurs when the velocity of the body decreases with time, i.e. the body slows down. In that case the acceleration is directed opposite to the direction of motion and is given a negative sign. For example, when brakes are applied to a moving car, it has negative acceleration.
questions.explanation: Definition, retardation = slowing down (acceleration opposite to motion), unit m/s^2.

questions.question: Write the three equations of motion for uniform acceleration and state the meaning of each symbol.
questions.answer:
For straight-line motion with uniform acceleration the three equations are:
  (1) v = u + at
  (2) s = ut + (1/2)at^2
  (3) v^2 = u^2 + 2as
Meaning of the symbols:
  u = initial velocity (m/s)
  v = final velocity (m/s)
  a = uniform acceleration (m/s^2)
  t = time interval (s)
  s = displacement covered in time t (m)
These equations are valid only when the acceleration a is constant (uniform). For retardation, a is taken as negative; for a body starting from rest, u = 0.
questions.explanation: List the three equations and define u, v, a, t, s.

questions.question: A car starting from rest accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s^2 for 6 s. Find (a) its final velocity and (b) the distance it travels in this time.
questions.answer:
Given: u = 0 (starts from rest), a = 4 m/s^2, t = 6 s.
(a) Using v = u + at:
   v = 0 + 4 x 6 = 24 m/s.
(b) Using s = ut + (1/2)at^2:
   s = 0 x 6 + (1/2) x 4 x 6^2 = (1/2) x 4 x 36 = 72 m.
So the final velocity is 24 m/s and the distance covered is 72 m.
(Check with v^2 = u^2 + 2as: 24^2 = 0 + 2 x 4 x 72 => 576 = 576, correct.)
questions.explanation: Apply v = u + at and s = ut + (1/2)at^2 with u = 0.

questions.question: A train moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 10 s by applying brakes. Find the retardation and the distance travelled before it stops.
questions.answer:
Given: u = 20 m/s, v = 0 (comes to rest), t = 10 s.
Retardation: a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 20)/10 = -2 m/s^2. So the retardation is 2 m/s^2.
Distance: use s = ut + (1/2)at^2:
   s = 20 x 10 + (1/2)(-2)(10^2) = 200 - 100 = 100 m.
(Check with v^2 = u^2 + 2as: 0 = 20^2 + 2(-2)s => 0 = 400 - 4s => s = 100 m.)
So the retardation is 2 m/s^2 and the train travels 100 m before stopping.
questions.explanation: a = (v-u)/t gives -2 m/s^2; s = 100 m by an equation of motion.

questions.question: Explain how a velocity-time graph is used to find (a) the acceleration and (b) the distance travelled. Illustrate with a body that accelerates uniformly from rest to velocity v in time t.
questions.answer:
On a velocity-time graph, velocity is plotted on the y-axis and time on the x-axis.
(a) ACCELERATION: The slope (gradient) of the velocity-time graph gives the acceleration, because acceleration = change in velocity / change in time. For uniform acceleration the graph is a straight sloping line; a steeper line means a larger acceleration. A horizontal line means zero acceleration (uniform velocity).
(b) DISTANCE: The area enclosed between the graph line and the time axis gives the distance (displacement) covered.
Illustration: A body starts from rest (u = 0) and accelerates uniformly to velocity v in time t. The graph is a straight line from the origin to the point (t, v).
 - Acceleration = slope = (v - 0)/(t - 0) = v/t.
 - Distance = area of the triangle under the line = (1/2) x base x height = (1/2) x t x v = (1/2)vt.
This matches s = ut + (1/2)at^2 with u = 0 and a = v/t, since (1/2)(v/t)t^2 = (1/2)vt. Thus the velocity-time graph gives both the acceleration (slope) and the distance (area).
questions.explanation: Slope = acceleration, area = distance; triangle area (1/2)vt for u = 0.

questions.question: Why is uniform circular motion called an accelerated motion even though the speed is constant?
questions.answer:
In uniform circular motion a body moves along a circle with constant SPEED. However, the DIRECTION of motion changes continuously, because at every point the velocity is directed along the tangent to the circle, and the tangent direction keeps turning.
Velocity is a VECTOR, defined by both magnitude and direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Since the direction of the velocity is changing continuously (even though its magnitude stays the same), the velocity itself is changing, and therefore the body is accelerating. Hence uniform circular motion is an accelerated motion. This is an important example showing that a body can be accelerated without any change in its speed.
questions.explanation: Constant speed but changing direction => changing velocity vector => acceleration.

questions.question: A body covers the first half of a journey at 30 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. The two halves are equal in distance. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
questions.answer:
Let each half of the journey have distance d, so the total distance = 2d.
Time for the first half: t1 = d / 30 hours.
Time for the second half: t2 = d / 60 hours.
Total time = t1 + t2 = d/30 + d/60 = 2d/60 + d/60 = 3d/60 = d/20 hours.
Average speed = total distance / total time = 2d / (d/20) = 2d x 20 / d = 40 km/h.
Note that the average speed (40 km/h) is NOT the simple mean of 30 and 60 (which would be 45 km/h); it is the harmonic-type average because equal distances, not equal times, are travelled at each speed.
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance / total time = 2d/(d/20) = 40 km/h.

questions.question: State whether each is a scalar or a vector, with a one-line reason: (a) distance, (b) displacement, (c) speed, (d) velocity, (e) acceleration.
questions.answer:
(a) Distance - SCALAR: it has only magnitude (a path length), no direction.
(b) Displacement - VECTOR: it has magnitude and a definite direction (initial to final position).
(c) Speed - SCALAR: it is distance per unit time, magnitude only.
(d) Velocity - VECTOR: it is displacement per unit time, so it has both magnitude and direction.
(e) Acceleration - VECTOR: it is the rate of change of velocity, which has magnitude and direction.
In short, distance and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.
questions.explanation: Scalars: distance, speed. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration.

questions.question: What is a frame of reference? Why is it needed to describe motion?
questions.answer: A frame of reference is a chosen object or origin (with a coordinate system attached) relative to which the position and motion of a body are measured. It is needed because position has no meaning by itself - it must be stated with respect to something. Since rest and motion are relative, the same body can be at rest in one frame and in motion in another, so a frame must always be specified to describe motion unambiguously.
questions.explanation: Definition + reason: motion is relative, so a reference is essential.

questions.question: What is a point object? Give one example.
questions.answer: A point object is a body whose size (dimensions) is negligibly small compared with the distance it travels, so that it can be treated as a single point for describing its motion. Treating a body as a point object simplifies the analysis, since we track only one position. Example: a train travelling between two cities hundreds of kilometres apart can be treated as a point object, because its length of a few hundred metres is negligible compared with the journey.
questions.explanation: Definition + example (train over a long journey).

questions.question: Give an example to show that an object can be at rest and in motion at the same time.
questions.answer: A passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus and to other passengers (her position does not change with respect to them). At the same instant she is in motion relative to a person standing on the road, because her position changes with respect to him. Thus the same object is simultaneously at rest in one frame and in motion in another, showing that rest and motion are relative.
questions.explanation: Bus passenger example: rest in one frame, motion in another.

questions.question: Define scalar and vector quantities with two examples of each.
questions.answer: A scalar quantity has only magnitude (a number with a unit). Examples: distance and speed (also mass, time, temperature). A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement and velocity (also acceleration, force). Two vectors are equal only if both their magnitude and direction are the same.
questions.explanation: Scalar = magnitude only; vector = magnitude + direction; examples.

questions.question: A person walks 6 m east, then 8 m north. Find the distance and the magnitude of displacement.
questions.answer:
Distance is the total path length = 6 + 8 = 14 m.
Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish. The two legs are perpendicular, so its magnitude = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 m, directed north-east. So distance = 14 m and displacement = 10 m.
questions.explanation: Distance 14 m; displacement = sqrt(6^2+8^2) = 10 m.

questions.question: Under what condition is the magnitude of displacement equal to the distance travelled?
questions.answer: The magnitude of displacement equals the distance travelled only when the body moves along a STRAIGHT LINE in a single direction, without reversing or turning. In that case the actual path is the same as the straight-line path from start to finish. If the body moves along a curved path, changes direction, or returns toward its start, the displacement becomes smaller than the distance.
questions.explanation: Only for straight-line motion in one direction without reversal.

questions.question: An athlete completes one full round of a circular track of radius r. What are the distance and displacement?
questions.answer: In one complete round, the athlete travels along the whole circumference, so the distance = 2*pi*r. However, the athlete ends at the same point from which she started, so the initial and final positions coincide and the displacement = 0. This illustrates that distance and displacement can be very different: distance can be large while displacement is zero for a closed path.
questions.explanation: Distance = 2*pi*r; displacement = 0 (returns to start).

questions.question: Define speed and average speed. Give the SI unit of speed.
questions.answer: Speed is the distance travelled by a body per unit time: speed = distance / time. It is a scalar quantity. Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey: average speed = total distance / total time. The SI unit of speed is metre per second (m/s).
questions.explanation: Definitions + SI unit m/s.

questions.question: A car travels 60 km in the first hour and 90 km in the next 2 hours. Find its average speed.
questions.answer:
Total distance = 60 + 90 = 150 km.
Total time = 1 + 2 = 3 hours.
Average speed = total distance / total time = 150 / 3 = 50 km/h.
questions.explanation: Average speed = 150 km / 3 h = 50 km/h.

questions.question: Convert (a) 90 km/h to m/s and (b) 15 m/s to km/h.
questions.answer:
(a) To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18: 90 x 5/18 = 450/18 = 25 m/s.
(b) To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5: 15 x 18/5 = 270/5 = 54 km/h.
So 90 km/h = 25 m/s and 15 m/s = 54 km/h.
questions.explanation: Use 5/18 and 18/5: 25 m/s and 54 km/h.

questions.question: Distinguish between uniform and non-uniform speed.
questions.answer: A body has uniform speed if it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, no matter how small the intervals are - its speed does not change. A body has non-uniform (variable) speed if it covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time - its speed keeps changing. For example, a car on an open highway with the cruise control set has nearly uniform speed, while a car in city traffic has non-uniform speed.
questions.explanation: Uniform = equal distances in equal times; non-uniform = unequal.

questions.question: Define velocity. How does it differ from speed?
questions.answer: Velocity is the displacement of a body per unit time, i.e. the rate of change of displacement: velocity = displacement / time. It is a vector quantity. It differs from speed in that speed is a scalar (distance per unit time, magnitude only) while velocity is a vector that also has a direction. The magnitude of velocity equals the speed only for straight-line motion without reversal.
questions.explanation: Velocity = displacement/time (vector); speed is scalar.

questions.question: A body moves 100 m east in 20 s and then 100 m west in 20 s. Find its average speed and average velocity.
questions.answer:
Total distance = 100 + 100 = 200 m. Total time = 20 + 20 = 40 s.
Average speed = total distance / total time = 200 / 40 = 5 m/s.
Displacement: 100 m east then 100 m west brings the body back to start, so net displacement = 0.
Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 0 / 40 = 0 m/s.
Thus average speed is 5 m/s but average velocity is 0, because the body returns to its starting point.
questions.explanation: Average speed 5 m/s; average velocity 0 (zero displacement).

questions.question: When is a body said to move with uniform velocity?
questions.answer: A body moves with uniform velocity when it travels in a STRAIGHT LINE and covers equal displacements in equal intervals of time - that is, both the magnitude (speed) AND the direction of its motion remain constant. If either the speed changes or the direction changes (as in circular motion), the velocity is non-uniform, even if the speed alone is constant.
questions.explanation: Uniform velocity = constant speed and constant direction (straight line).

questions.question: Define acceleration and give its SI unit.
questions.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity of a body with time. If the velocity changes from u to v in time t, then acceleration a = (v - u)/t. It is a vector quantity, directed along the change in velocity. Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m/s^2).
questions.explanation: a = (v - u)/t; unit m/s^2.

questions.question: A motorcycle's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration.
questions.answer:
Given u = 5 m/s, v = 25 m/s, t = 4 s.
Acceleration a = (v - u)/t = (25 - 5)/4 = 20/4 = 5 m/s^2.
Since a is positive and in the direction of motion, the motorcycle is speeding up.

questions.question: Distinguish between positive acceleration and retardation.
questions.answer: Positive acceleration occurs when the velocity of a body increases with time; the acceleration is in the same direction as the motion and the body speeds up. Retardation (negative acceleration or deceleration) occurs when the velocity decreases with time; the acceleration is directed opposite to the motion and the body slows down. For example, a car speeding up has positive acceleration; the same car braking has retardation.
questions.explanation: Positive accel = speeding up; retardation = slowing down (opposite direction).

questions.question: Distinguish between uniform and non-uniform acceleration.
questions.answer: A body has uniform acceleration if its velocity changes by EQUAL amounts in equal intervals of time - the acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction. A freely falling body (acceleration g) is an example. A body has non-uniform acceleration if its velocity changes by UNEQUAL amounts in equal intervals - the acceleration itself keeps changing. A car in stop-and-go traffic has non-uniform acceleration.
questions.explanation: Uniform = equal velocity change per equal time; non-uniform = unequal.

questions.question: Write the three equations of motion.
questions.answer:
For straight-line motion with uniform acceleration:
(1) v = u + at
(2) s = ut + (1/2)at^2
(3) v^2 = u^2 + 2as
Here u is the initial velocity, v the final velocity, a the (uniform) acceleration, t the time and s the displacement.
questions.explanation: List v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as.

questions.question: State the meaning of each symbol in the equation s = ut + (1/2)at^2.
questions.answer: In s = ut + (1/2)at^2: s is the displacement covered in time t; u is the initial velocity (velocity at the start, when t = 0); a is the uniform acceleration; t is the time interval over which the motion is considered. The term ut is the displacement that would occur at constant velocity u, and (1/2)at^2 is the extra displacement produced by the acceleration. The equation is valid only when a is constant.
questions.explanation: Define s, u, a, t and the meaning of the two terms.

questions.question: A car starting from rest attains a velocity of 18 m/s in 6 s. Find its acceleration and the distance travelled.
A train moving at 72 km/h is brought to rest over 200 m. Find the retardation.
questions.answer:
First convert: u = 72 km/h = 72 x 5/18 = 20 m/s. The train stops, so v = 0, and s = 200 m.
Use v^2 = u^2 + 2as:
   0 = 20^2 + 2a(200)
   0 = 400 + 400a
   400a = -400
   a = -1 m/s^2.
So the retardation is 1 m/s^2 (the negative sign shows the velocity is decreasing).
questions.explanation: Convert to 20 m/s; v^2 = u^2 + 2as gives a = -1 m/s^2.

questions.question: A stone is dropped from a height and hits the ground after 4 s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, find the height and the velocity with which it strikes the ground.
questions.answer:
The stone is dropped, so u = 0; a = g = 9.8 m/s^2; t = 4 s.
Height: s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = 0 + (1/2)(9.8)(4^2) = (1/2)(9.8)(16) = 78.4 m.
Final velocity: v = u + at = 0 + 9.8 x 4 = 39.2 m/s.
So the height is 78.4 m and it strikes the ground at 39.2 m/s.

questions.question: A bus accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s while covering 200 m. Find its acceleration.
questions.answer:
Given u = 10 m/s, v = 30 m/s, s = 200 m.
Use v^2 = u^2 + 2as:
   30^2 = 10^2 + 2a(200)
   900 = 100 + 400a
   400a = 800
   a = 2 m/s^2.
So the acceleration is 2 m/s^2.

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with a velocity of 19.6 m/s. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, find the time to reach the highest point and the maximum height.
questions.answer:
Going up, u = 19.6 m/s and a = -g = -9.8 m/s^2. At the highest point v = 0.
Time: v = u + at => 0 = 19.6 - 9.8t => t = 19.6/9.8 = 2 s.
Maximum height: v^2 = u^2 + 2as => 0 = 19.6^2 - 2(9.8)s => 2(9.8)s = 384.16 => s = 384.16/19.6 = 19.6 m.
So the ball takes 2 s to reach the top and rises 19.6 m.
questions.explanation: t = u/g = 2 s; height = u^2/(2g) = 19.6 m.

questions.question: What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent? What does a horizontal line mean?
questions.answer: The slope of a distance-time graph (change in distance divided by change in time) represents the SPEED of the body. A steeper slope means a greater speed. A horizontal straight line (zero slope) means the distance is not changing with time, i.e. the body is AT REST.
questions.explanation: Slope = speed; horizontal line = body at rest.

questions.question: What do the slope and the area of a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.answer: On a velocity-time graph: the SLOPE (change in velocity divided by change in time) gives the ACCELERATION of the body - a steeper line means a larger acceleration, and a horizontal line means zero acceleration. The AREA enclosed between the graph line and the time axis gives the DISTANCE (displacement) travelled by the body in that time interval. These two facts allow the equations of motion to be derived graphically.
questions.explanation: Slope = acceleration; area = distance.

questions.question: Why is uniform circular motion an example of accelerated motion?
questions.answer: In uniform circular motion a body moves along a circle at constant speed. Although the speed (magnitude of velocity) is constant, the DIRECTION of motion changes continuously, because the velocity is always tangent to the circle and the tangent keeps turning. Since velocity is a vector, a change in its direction is a change in velocity, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Therefore the body is accelerating even though its speed never changes.
questions.explanation: Constant speed but continuously changing direction => changing velocity => acceleration.

questions.question: What does a horizontal straight line on a velocity-time graph tell you about the motion of the body?
questions.answer: A horizontal straight line on a velocity-time graph means the velocity stays the same at every instant - it does not change with time. So the body is moving with CONSTANT (uniform) velocity, and because the velocity is not changing, its acceleration is ZERO. (If the horizontal line lies along the time axis at v = 0, it would instead mean the body is at rest.)
questions.explanation: Horizontal v-t line = constant velocity, zero acceleration.

questions.question: A body moves in a circle of radius 14 m and completes one revolution in 22 s. Find its speed. (Take pi = 22/7.)
questions.answer:
In one revolution the body covers the circumference = 2*pi*r = 2 x (22/7) x 14 = 2 x 22 x 2 = 88 m, in time T = 22 s.
Speed v = circumference / period = 88 / 22 = 4 m/s.
Note that although the speed is constant at 4 m/s, the motion is still accelerated because the direction keeps changing.

questions.question: A student leaves home and walks 30 m east to a shop, then 40 m north to a friend's house. Answer: (a) What total distance did she walk? (b) What is the magnitude of her displacement? (c) Is displacement a scalar or a vector? (d) If she returns home by the same route, what is her displacement for the whole trip?
questions.answer:
(a) Distance = 30 + 40 = 70 m (the actual path length).
(b) The two legs are perpendicular, so displacement magnitude = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 m (directed north-east).
(c) Displacement is a VECTOR quantity (it has both magnitude and direction).
(d) If she returns home, her final position is the same as her starting position, so the net displacement for the whole trip is ZERO (although the total distance walked would be 140 m).
questions.explanation: Distance 70 m; displacement 50 m; vector; round trip displacement 0.

questions.question: A car travels from town A to town B. It covers the first 60 km in 1 hour, then stops for 30 minutes, then covers the next 60 km in 1.5 hours. Answer: (a) What is the total distance? (b) What is the total time including the stop? (c) What is the average speed for the whole journey? (d) Was the speed uniform? Justify.
questions.answer:
(a) Total distance = 60 + 60 = 120 km.
(b) Total time = 1 h + 0.5 h (stop) + 1.5 h = 3 hours.
(c) Average speed = total distance / total time = 120 / 3 = 40 km/h.
(d) The speed was NOT uniform. In the first part the speed was 60 km/h, during the stop it was 0, and in the last part it was 60/1.5 = 40 km/h. Since the car covered unequal distances in equal time intervals (and even stopped), its speed changed during the journey, so the motion was non-uniform.
questions.explanation: Distance 120 km; time 3 h; average speed 40 km/h; non-uniform.

questions.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s^2. Answer: (a) Find its velocity after 8 s. (b) Find the distance covered in 8 s. (c) After 8 s the driver applies brakes and the car stops in 4 s. Find the retardation. (d) Find the distance covered during braking.
questions.answer:
Acceleration phase: u = 0, a = 2 m/s^2, t = 8 s.
(a) v = u + at = 0 + 2 x 8 = 16 m/s.
(b) s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = 0 + (1/2)(2)(8^2) = (1/2)(2)(64) = 64 m.
Braking phase: u = 16 m/s, v = 0, t = 4 s.
(c) retardation a = (v - u)/t = (0 - 16)/4 = -4 m/s^2, i.e. retardation of 4 m/s^2.
(d) distance s = (u + v)/2 * t = (16 + 0)/2 * 4 = 32 m. So during braking the car travels 32 m.
questions.explanation: v = 16 m/s; s = 64 m; retardation 4 m/s^2; braking distance 32 m.

questions.question: The velocity-time graph of a body is a straight line starting at 0 m/s and rising to 20 m/s over 10 s, after which it stays constant at 20 m/s for the next 5 s. Answer: (a) What is the acceleration during the first 10 s? (b) What is the acceleration during the next 5 s? (c) What distance is covered in the first 10 s? (d) What type of motion occurs in the last 5 s?
questions.answer:
(a) Acceleration in the first 10 s = slope = (20 - 0)/(10 - 0) = 2 m/s^2.
(b) In the next 5 s the velocity is constant (horizontal line), so the slope is zero: acceleration = 0.
(c) Distance in first 10 s = area under the line = area of triangle = (1/2)(base)(height) = (1/2)(10)(20) = 100 m.
(d) In the last 5 s the body moves with constant (uniform) velocity of 20 m/s, i.e. uniform motion in a straight line with zero acceleration.
questions.explanation: a = 2 m/s^2 then 0; distance 100 m; last phase uniform velocity.

questions.question: A train's velocity changes as follows: it speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s, runs at 20 m/s for 30 s, then slows to rest in 5 s. Answer: (a) Find the acceleration in the first phase. (b) Find the acceleration (retardation) in the last phase. (c) What is the acceleration in the middle phase? (d) Which phase shows the greatest magnitude of acceleration?
questions.answer:
(a) First phase: a = (20 - 0)/10 = 2 m/s^2.
(b) Last phase: a = (0 - 20)/5 = -4 m/s^2, i.e. a retardation of 4 m/s^2.
(c) Middle phase: velocity is constant at 20 m/s, so the change in velocity is zero and acceleration = 0.
(d) The last phase has the greatest magnitude of acceleration (4 m/s^2) compared with 2 m/s^2 in the first phase and 0 in the middle.
questions.explanation: a = 2, 0, -4 m/s^2; last phase has the largest magnitude.

questions.question: Two friends, Asha and Bina, are sitting in a train moving at 60 km/h. A man stands on the platform. Answer: (a) Is Asha at rest or in motion relative to Bina? (b) Is Asha at rest or in motion relative to the man on the platform? (c) Can we say Asha is 'absolutely' at rest? (d) What concept does this illustrate?
questions.answer:
(a) Relative to Bina (who is in the same train), Asha's position does not change, so Asha is AT REST relative to Bina.
(b) Relative to the man on the platform, Asha's position changes with time, so Asha is IN MOTION (at 60 km/h) relative to him.
(c) No - there is no absolute rest. Even the platform is on the Earth, which is rotating and orbiting the Sun.
(d) This illustrates that rest and motion are RELATIVE: they depend on the chosen frame of reference.
questions.explanation: Rest vs Bina; motion vs man; no absolute rest; rest/motion are relative.

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with an initial speed of 30 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s^2 and ignore air resistance. Answer: (a) How long does it take to reach the highest point? (b) What is the maximum height reached? (c) What is its velocity when it returns to the ground? (d) What is the total time of flight?
questions.answer:
Upward: u = 30 m/s, a = -10 m/s^2.
(a) At the top v = 0: 0 = 30 - 10t => t = 3 s.
(b) Max height: v^2 = u^2 + 2as => 0 = 900 - 2(10)s => 20s = 900 => s = 45 m.
(c) By symmetry (or energy), it returns to the ground with the same speed it was thrown, 30 m/s, but directed downward.
(d) Total time of flight = time up + time down = 3 + 3 = 6 s.
questions.explanation: t_up = 3 s; height 45 m; returns at 30 m/s; total flight 6 s.

questions.question: An athlete runs once around a circular track of circumference 400 m in 50 s, finishing where she started. Answer: (a) What total distance did she cover? (b) What is her displacement? (c) What is her average speed? (d) What is her average velocity? Explain the difference.
questions.answer:
(a) Distance = full circumference = 400 m.
(b) She finishes where she started, so the displacement = 0.
(c) Average speed = total distance / total time = 400 / 50 = 8 m/s.
(d) Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 0 / 50 = 0 m/s.
The difference arises because speed depends on the path length (distance), which is 400 m, while velocity depends on displacement, which is zero for a closed loop. So she has a non-zero average speed but a zero average velocity.
questions.explanation: Distance 400 m; displacement 0; avg speed 8 m/s; avg velocity 0.

questions.question: A car moves along a straight road. Its distance-time graph is a straight sloping line for the first part of the journey and then becomes a horizontal line. Answer: (a) What does the sloping straight line tell us about the motion? (b) What does the horizontal portion tell us? (c) How would you find the speed from the sloping part? (d) Sketch in words what a velocity-time graph for the sloping part would look like.
questions.answer:
(a) A straight sloping line on a distance-time graph means the distance increases steadily with time, i.e. the car moves with UNIFORM SPEED (constant speed).
(b) A horizontal line means the distance is not changing with time, i.e. the car is AT REST (it has stopped).
(c) The speed equals the slope of the sloping line = (change in distance)/(change in time); pick two points on the line and divide the rise by the run.
(d) Since the speed is constant during the sloping part, the velocity-time graph for that part would be a HORIZONTAL straight line (constant velocity, zero acceleration).
questions.explanation: Sloping = uniform speed; horizontal = at rest; speed = slope; v-t graph horizontal.

questions.question: A scooter moving at 15 m/s accelerates uniformly at 1 m/s^2 for 10 s. Answer: (a) Find its final velocity. (b) Find the distance covered in these 10 s. (c) Express the final velocity in km/h. (d) If it had instead continued at 15 m/s, how far would it have gone in 10 s?
questions.answer:
Given u = 15 m/s, a = 1 m/s^2, t = 10 s.
(a) v = u + at = 15 + 1 x 10 = 25 m/s.
(b) s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = 15 x 10 + (1/2)(1)(10^2) = 150 + 50 = 200 m.
(c) 25 m/s = 25 x 18/5 = 90 km/h.
(d) At a constant 15 m/s for 10 s: distance = speed x time = 15 x 10 = 150 m (which is 50 m less than the accelerated case, the extra being the (1/2)at^2 term).
questions.explanation: v = 25 m/s; s = 200 m; 90 km/h; constant-speed distance 150 m.
